newsitem.title: RUSSIA: World markets watch timing of Yeltsin heart op.
newsitem.headline: World markets watch timing of Yeltsin heart op.

text.p: Doctors meet on Monday to decide when to operate on Russian President Boris Yeltsin amid indications, based on political and economic factors as much as medical evidence, that they could choose this week.

Yeltsin said on September 5 he would have an operation on his heart, but doctors said at the end of that month it would take 6-10 weeks to prepare him for surgery -- a bypass operation to improve blood supply to the heart.

The six week deadline comes to an end this week and U.S. specialist Michael DeBakey, who carried out the world's first successful heart bypass operation, said before leaving for Moscow for Monday's meeting that he expected the operation to take place soon.

Among factors seen as lending weight to an early operation are the U.S. presidential election on Tuesday, which will focus attention elsewhere, and public holidays in Russia keeping domestic media attention low and Russia's nervous financial markets closed.
Russian markets are closed on Thursday and Friday for public holidays marking the anniversary of the Bolshevik Revolution and there will be no newspapers until early next week.
A successful operation could give the local share market a lift next week just in time for a major roadshow expected to tell international markets about Russia's planned Eurobond.

The roadshow, which starts in Tokyo on November 11, will officially deal with the state of the Russian economy. But markets expect news about the bond, tipped to be for up to $500 million at something more than 300 basis points over five-year U.S. Treasuries.
It will be the first time Moscow has tapped debt markets as a sovereign borrower since the 1917 Bolshevik Revolution brought the communists to power.
Russia's domestic economic picture is far from clear. Inflation is low and the budget deficit is under control, but wage arrears have reached new heights and tax revenues are far too low.
The International Monetary Fund pulled its latest mission out of Russia without recommending the release of a tranche of a $10 billion three-year loan because it was worried about low tax collection.
Dealers have said Yeltsin's health should not affect Russia's decision to go ahead with the bond issue even though markets have watched the president anxiously in the last few months.
"Russia is larger than Yeltsin," one Frankfurt-based eastern European specialist said last month. "There are more people than one who are competent to replace Yeltsin."
However news last week that DeBakey would head for Moscow supported Russian share prices because dealers realised their long wait for news about the president could be coming to an end.

Yeltsin virtually disappeared from the public eye before the July 3 second round of the Russian presidential election and has spent the last four months in a sanatorium outside Moscow, in the exclusive Central Clinical Hospital and -- very occasionally -- in the Kremlin.
